title: What goes into a change request
blurb: Know every field a change request should capture and record, and explain why each one matters.
question: The train operator emails Millbrook's project manager: 'Please add a lift to platform 2.' Before this can be evaluated, what should the change request capture, and what will be added to it as it moves through change control?

teach.h: The record that starts change control
teach.body: A change request is the formal record of a proposed change to the project's agreed baseline. It describes the change, explains why it is wanted and gives a first view of its impact, so it can be evaluated and decided. In plain English: it turns a remark in a corridor into something that can be tracked, judged and audited. Each request is listed in the change log, and the request itself is updated with the decision as it moves through the process.

teach.caption: The first three groups are completed when the request is raised. The outcome is recorded as it passes through the process.

head: Field
Millbrook CR-031
rows: Do nothing, shaft only, full lift
teach.caption: Figures are kept rough on purpose: the initial estimate supports a quick screen, not a final decision.

teach.h: Why each field earns its place
teach.body: The reference, date and requester make the request traceable and let the PM go back for detail and report the outcome. The description, reason and benefits let the decision be tested against the business case. The initial impact estimate, priority and options make the initial evaluation quick and fair. Affected items link to the configuration records so nothing is missed. The decision, approver, date and status complete the audit trail and show that the right authority decided.

teach.h: The status field over a request's life
teach.caption: A typical set of status values. The status, kept current in the change log, lets anyone see where every request has got to.
Raising a request includes logging it, so each request appears in the log from day one.

rows.label: 'Add a lift please' in an email
No reference, so it can't be traced
Rough impact on time, cost and risk

teach.note: A poor request either stalls at initial evaluation or, worse, slips through without anyone knowing its impact.

teach.text: Exam traps: a change request is not just 'what I want'. It must also record WHY (reason and benefits) and a first view of the IMPACT. It does not contain the updated baseline or the detailed design: those come after approval. And don't confuse it with the risk register (uncertain events) or the issue log (problems that have happened), although an issue can lead to a change request.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Identification: unique reference, date and requester, for traceability.
Description of the change plus its reason and benefits, so it can be judged against the business case.
Initial impact estimate on time, cost, scope, quality and risk, plus priority or urgency.
Options considered and affected items (linked to configuration records).
Later: decision, approver, date and status, completing the audit trail.
A change request is the formal record of a proposed change to the baseline.
Identify it: unique reference, date, requester.
Describe and justify it: the change, the reason, the benefits.
First view of impact: time, cost, scope, quality and risk, plus priority, options and affected items.
Record the outcome: decision, approver, date and status, tracked in the change log.

summary: You can now list what a change request should capture when it is raised and what is recorded on it as it is decided. You can also explain why each field matters for traceability, a fair evaluation and a sound audit trail.

A.q: Why does every change request need a unique reference?
options: So the requester can approve it later
So it can be traced to its decision
So its cost is fixed when it is raised
So it can skip the initial evaluation
A.why: A unique reference lets the request be tracked in the change log and traced from being raised through to its decision and implementation.

whyNot.0: Requesters do not approve their own changes.
whyNot.2: Cost is estimated and assessed; a reference does not fix it.
whyNot.3: Every request is screened; a reference does not exempt it.

A.q: Which of the following is NOT normally recorded on a change request?
options: The reason for making the change
The initial impact estimate
Lessons from project closure
The priority or the urgency
A.why: Lessons from closure belong in the lessons log or closure report. The other three are standard change request fields.

whyNot.0: The reason (justification) is a core field.
whyNot.1: An initial estimate of impact is captured so the request can be screened.
whyNot.3: Priority or urgency is captured so requests can be handled in a sensible order.

A.q: Which change request fields most directly link the request to the business case?
options: Its reason and expected benefits
Its reference and its status
The date and the requester's name
The affected configuration items
A.why: The reason and benefits show what the change would contribute, so the decision can be tested against the business case and objectives.

whyNot.1: Reference and status support tracking, not justification.
whyNot.2: Date and requester identify the request; they do not justify it.
whyNot.3: Affected items show what the change touches, not why it is worth doing.

B.q: Why is the requester's name recorded on a change request?
options: So they can approve their own change
So the cost is charged to their own team
So the request jumps to the top of the list
So they can clarify it and hear the outcome
B.why: Knowing who raised the request lets the PM clarify it during evaluation and tell them the decision and its reasons.

whyNot.0: Requesters do not approve their own changes.
whyNot.1: Recharging may happen in some organisations, but it is not why the name is recorded.
whyNot.2: Priority depends on urgency and value, not on who asked.

B.q: Recording the 'affected items' on a change request mainly helps the project team to…
options: decide who should approve the change
find the configuration items it touches
set the priority and urgency of the request
explain the benefit of the change
B.why: Affected items link the request to the configuration records, so the team knows which products, drawings or documents would need to change.

whyNot.0: The approver depends on the governance and delegated authority, not on affected items.
whyNot.2: Priority and urgency are separate fields.
whyNot.3: Benefits are recorded in their own field.

B.q: Once a change request has been decided, which details are added to it?
options: Reference, requester, date and reason
Benefits, options, priority and urgency
Decision, approver, date and status
Lessons, owner, budget and risk score
B.why: After the decision, the request records what was decided, who decided it, when, and its new status.

whyNot.0: These are captured when the request is first raised.
whyNot.1: These are also captured when it is raised, to support evaluation.
whyNot.3: These are not the standard outcome fields of a change request.

C.q: Millbrook's sponsor receives a request that reads only: 'Please add a lift to platform 2.' What is the most important information missing for an initial evaluation?
options: The reason, benefits and a rough impact
A full detailed design of the new lift
The approved and updated baseline plan
Confirmation that the lift is installed
C.why: Without a reason, benefits and an initial impact estimate, nobody can judge quickly whether the request is worth a full assessment.

whyNot.1: Detailed design is not needed to raise a request; it may follow if the change is approved.
whyNot.2: The baseline is only updated after approval.
whyNot.3: Installation is the end of the process, not something a request contains.

C.q: Which THREE are typically captured when a change request is first raised? 1. A description of the change 2. Its priority or urgency 3. The rebaselined schedule 4. The options considered
options: 1, 2 and 3
1, 3 and 4
2, 3 and 4
1, 2 and 4
C.why: The description (1), priority or urgency (2) and options considered (4) are captured when the request is raised. A rebaselined schedule (3) only exists after approval.

whyNot.0: A rebaselined schedule (3) is produced at the update plans stage, after approval.
whyNot.1: A rebaselined schedule (3) comes after approval, and this misses priority (2).
whyNot.2: A rebaselined schedule (3) comes after approval, and this misses the description (1).

C.q: After Millbrook is complete, an auditor asks why the budget rose by £120k in month 9. Which record would answer this most fully?
options: The original approved business case
The approved change request
The project's risk register entries
The stakeholder map for the station
C.why: The change request records the change, its justification, its impact and who approved it and when: the audit trail behind the budget increase.

whyNot.0: The original business case predates the change, so it cannot explain the rise.
whyNot.2: The risk register records uncertain events, not approved changes and their justification.
whyNot.3: A stakeholder map shows interests and influence, not budget decisions.

reteach.title: Think of a house extension
reteach.question: Your builder is halfway through a kitchen extension. You decide you want a roof lantern as well. What should the builder write down before anyone prices it, and what gets added later?

blocks.body: A good builder writes a variation sheet: a number (V4), the date, and that you asked. What you want: a roof lantern over the dining area. Why: more light. A rough idea of cost and delay, how soon you need an answer, and the options (lantern, two Velux windows, or nothing). What it affects: roof drawings and the steel order. Later, the sheet records 'agreed', who agreed, and when.

blocks.text: Without the sheet, the final bill arrives with an extra line nobody remembers agreeing. The record protects both sides.

explain.body: A unique reference, the date raised and the requester's name. Together they make the request traceable in the change log, and let the PM go back to the requester for detail and report the outcome.

test.q: Which set of fields identifies a change request?
options: Options, priority and impact
Decision, approver and status
Reference, date and requester
Reason, benefits and description
test.why: Reference, date and requester identify the request and make it traceable.

whyNot.0: These give a first view of impact rather than identifying the request.
whyNot.1: These record the outcome, after the decision.
whyNot.3: These describe and justify the change.

explain.body: A clear description of the change, the reason it is needed and the benefits it should bring. This is what allows the change to be judged against the business case and the project objectives.

test.q: Why must a change request state the reason for the change?
options: So it can be judged against the business case
So its configuration items can be labelled
So the requester's line manager can be informed
So the change can be implemented sooner
test.why: The reason (with the benefits) lets the decision-maker test the change against the business case and objectives.

whyNot.1: Labelling configuration items is part of configuration management, not the reason field.
whyNot.2: Informing managers is a communication matter, not the purpose of the reason.
whyNot.3: A reason does not speed anything up; the change still needs evaluating and approving.

explain.body: An initial impact estimate (time, cost, scope, quality and risk), the priority or urgency, the options considered and the affected items. Rough is fine: this lets the initial evaluation be quick and fair, and points the detailed evaluation at the right items.

test.q: What is the main purpose of the initial impact estimate on a change request?
options: To set the final price agreed with suppliers
To replace the need for a detailed evaluation
To update the baseline before the decision
To support a quick and fair initial screen
test.why: A rough estimate of time, cost, scope, quality and risk lets the initial evaluation decide whether a full assessment is worthwhile.

whyNot.0: Final prices come later, if at all; this is only a rough estimate.
whyNot.1: A worthwhile request still gets a detailed evaluation.
whyNot.2: The baseline is updated only after approval.

explain.h: Record the outcome, track it in the log
explain.body: As the request is decided, it records the decision, the approver, the date and its status. The change log lists every request with its reference, summary and status, so the PM can track and report all changes at once.

test.q: How does the change log differ from an individual change request?
options: The log holds the full design of each change
The log lists all requests and their status
The log is only created once a change is approved
The log records uncertain events and their owners
test.why: The change log is the register of all change requests, showing each one's reference, summary, status and decision.

whyNot.0: Neither the log nor the request holds the full design.
whyNot.2: Requests are logged when raised, not just when approved.
whyNot.3: Uncertain events and owners belong in the risk register.
